text: Every popular-science article calls entanglement spooky, but you need the precise, checkable definition: a multi-qubit state is entangled exactly when it cannot be written as a tensor product of independent single-qubit states. No mysticism — just a factoring question you can actually verify.

Take two qubits prepared completely independently, each put through its own Hadamard gate. The combined state is ket-plus tensor ket-plus, which multiplies out to one-quarter on each of the four two-qubit outcomes — normalized, since four quarters sum to 1. This state factors cleanly: qubit 1 is in ket-plus, qubit 2 is in ket-plus, completely independently. Measure one and you learn nothing new about the other. This is the boring case.

Now compare that to ket-Phi-plus, which is ket-00 plus ket-11 over root 2. Assume it could be factored the same way: that requires a-times-c equal to one over root 2, a-times-d equal to zero, b-times-c equal to zero, and b-times-d equal to one over root 2. Since a-times-c isn't zero, neither a nor c can be zero. Since b-times-d isn't zero, neither b nor d can be zero. But a-times-d equal zero requires a or d to be zero — and neither is. That's a direct contradiction. No choice of a, b, c, d works, for any values whatsoever.

This isn't a notational curiosity — it's the dividing line between two qubits and one genuinely joint quantum object. A product state never gives you anything a pair of independent classical coins couldn't eventually imitate. An unfactorizable state like Phi-plus cannot be reduced to two independent objects under any circumstances, and this non-factorizability is the actual resource that algorithms, teleportation, and quantum cryptography are built on.

The recipe for testing any two-qubit state is always the same: write the general product-state form, expand it, and try to match coefficients against the state you're given. A consistent solution means a product state; a contradictory system of equations means entangled. You'll use exactly this technique in lesson 20's problem-solving lab.
